strengths: Well-motivated formulation: Decoupling general behavior prior modeling (via autoregressive next-token prediction on large-scale expert logs) from safety and feasibility alignment (via RL fine-tuning) is a principled approach to overcoming noisy/suboptimal demonstrations (e.g., speeding, near-misses) in autonomous driving.

Clever dual-model rollout mechanism: Using the frozen pretrained predictor as a reactive multi-agent world simulator while optimizing the ego policy maintains realistic dynamic interactions without destabilizing non-ego behaviors during policy exploration.

Strong empirical results on nuPlan: Plan-R1 achieves state-of-the-art closed-loop reactive scores (R-CLS) on standard benchmarks (Val14, Test14-hard, Test14-random), notably outperforming both pure imitation learning planners (PLUTO) and generative planners (Diffusion Planner).

Insightful ablations and analyses: The paper provides informative evaluations including metric breakdowns (TTC, drivable area, speed compliance), the effect of KL regularization weight, and a Pass@k analysis demonstrating improved trajectory feasibility under multi-sampling.
weaknesses: Missing details on rule-based reward formulation: Since alignment with explicit planning principles is central to the framework, relegating the definitions, thresholds, and weights of the reward terms entirely to the supplementary material limits the self-containment of the main manuscript.

Lack of inference runtime and latency analysis: Autoregressive token-by-token decoding across both the ego vehicle and surrounding agents can be computationally demanding. Autonomous driving typically operates under strict real-time constraints (e.g., 10 Hz replanning), but no latency benchmarks or computational overhead figures are reported.

Limited algorithmic comparison for sequence fine-tuning: While the paper justifies GRPO primarily for its critic-free simplicity and stability, there is no direct empirical comparison against alternative alignment methods (e.g., PPO, DPO, or reward-guided sampling/re-ranking) to demonstrate why GRPO specifically is the superior choice for motion token alignment.

strengths: Clear and timely conceptual formulation adapting the two-stage LLM paradigm (next-token autoregressive pretraining followed by GRPO reinforcement learning alignment) to autonomous vehicle trajectory planning.

The dual-model rollout mechanism—freezing the pretrained model as a reactive multi-agent world model while fine-tuning the ego vehicle policy—elegantly enables multi-agent interaction during RL without needing complex external simulators or destabilizing surrounding agent dynamics.

Strong closed-loop simulation performance on the competitive nuPlan benchmark, notably achieving significant gains in reactive closed-loop scores (R-CLS) across Val14, Test14-hard, and Test14-random over existing imitation and diffusion baselines.
Well-structured ablations and qualitative examples demonstrating that RL fine-tuning successfully filters out unsafe demonstrations (e.g., speeding and collisions) and improves the pass@k metric.
weaknesses: The individual technical components are mostly direct adaptations from existing work: trajectory tokenization and factorized attention decoders follow MotionLM/Trajeglish/SMART, and the RL fine-tuning directly applies GRPO with standard rule-based driving metrics.
Important technical details regarding the reward formulation (Eq. 4) are omitted from the main text with a reference to an Appendix that is not attached to the manuscript.

There is no discussion or empirical measurement of inference latency and computational overhead. Autoregressive token-by-token multi-agent rollout can be computationally expensive and latency-sensitive for real-time autonomous driving deployment.

On the Test14-hard split with post-processing (Table 1), Plan-R1* slightly underperforms Diffusion Planner* under both non-reactive (77.79 vs. 78.87) and reactive (80.97 vs. 82.00) settings; further discussion or analysis of this difficult split would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Clear problem motivation: The paper convincingly identifies and demonstrates the limitation of relying solely on imitation learning from human demonstrations in nuPlan, where suboptimal behaviors (e.g., speeding and low TTC) are inherited by the planner.

Well-structured framework: The two-stage paradigm (autoregressive motion token pretraining followed by RL alignment via GRPO with rule-based safety rewards) provides a clean way to decouple distribution modeling from safety alignment without requiring costly human preference annotations.

Strong closed-loop benchmark results: The proposed method demonstrates consistent and notable improvements in reactive closed-loop simulation (R-CLS) on nuPlan (Val14, Test14-hard, Test14-random) over strong learning-based baselines such as PLUTO and Diffusion Planner.

Informative ablation studies: The breakdown of sub-metric improvements (Table 2), the sensitivity analysis of the KL regularization parameter (Figure 4), and the Pass@k analysis (Figure 5) provide useful insights into the fine-tuning behavior.
weaknesses: Misaligned / trendy branding vs. technical novelty: The paper borrows the 'R1' moniker from recent reasoning LLMs (e.g., DeepSeek-R1), but the method does not introduce reasoning traces, test-time compute scaling, or self-reflection. It is fundamentally standard discrete trajectory tokenization (following Trajeglish/MotionLM) combined with GRPO using classical rule-based driving cost functions.

Omission of critical implementation details and appendix: Key mathematical and implementation details—including the exact formulation of the multiplicative safety terms and soft cost weights in Equation (4), token vocabulary construction, and training hyperparameters—are deferred to an appendix that is not included in the manuscript.

Unaddressed real-time feasibility and inference latency: Autoregressive token-by-token generation for ego and surrounding agents is computationally demanding. Trajectory planning in autonomous driving strictly requires high-frequency execution (e.g., 10 Hz), but no latency, throughput, or model parameter complexity comparisons are provided.

Potential distribution shift in the dual-model simulator: Using a frozen autoregressive model as the interactive world model during RL exploration introduces risks of out-of-distribution compounding errors when the ego explores novel trajectories, which is neither analyzed nor ablated.

strengths: Clear and compelling motivation: Decoupling general behavior learning (via autoregressive next-token prediction on expert trajectories) from explicit principle alignment (safety, comfort, and rule compliance via RL) effectively overcomes key limitations of expert demonstrations, such as rare safety-critical events and inherited suboptimal behaviors (e.g., speeding).

Insightful analysis and algorithmic adaptation: The authors convincingly identify why standard GRPO fails in multi-objective trajectory planning—group-wise variance normalization squashes large penalty scales of rare safety violations to match small fluctuations in safe groups. The proposed Variance-Decoupled GRPO (VD-GRPO) is simple, well-justified, and directly addresses this imbalance.

Strong empirical performance: Plan-R1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the competitive nuPlan closed-loop benchmark, exhibiting notable gains over strong baselines (e.g., PLUTO, Diffusion Planner) particularly in the reactive setting (R-CLS) on both random and hard test splits.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation and ablations: The ablation studies thoroughly examine the contribution of each design component, including the dual-model reactive rollout vs. ground-truth replay, the impact of model capacity, reward function components, group size, and key hyperparameters (beta and c).
weaknesses: Incremental algorithmic novelty: The individual components—discrete tokenization (MotionLM/Trajeglish), autoregressive trajectory generation, and RL alignment with modified GRPO (closely related to unnormalized variants like Dr.GRPO)—are adaptations of existing methods, although their integration and domain-specific formulation are well executed.

Inference latency and computational overhead: Generating trajectories token-by-token autoregressively can introduce latency concerns in real-time autonomous driving compared to single-shot continuous planners. The paper would benefit from reporting the wall-clock runtime/planning frequency (Hz) during closed-loop rollout.

Potential world model distribution shift: The dual-model setup relies on a frozen pre-trained predictor to simulate surrounding agents' responses during RL exploration. When the ego policy explores unusual or out-of-distribution behaviors during training, the accuracy and fidelity of this reactive world model are not explicitly evaluated or bounded.

Potential risk of metric alignment/reward overlap: The rule-based rewards (collision, drivable area, comfort, speed compliance) closely mirror the nuPlan benchmark evaluation metrics. A brief discussion or validation on whether the policy exhibits any subtle reward-hacking behaviors would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated framework that addresses key shortcomings of imitation learning in autonomous driving (e.g., inheriting unsafe behaviors such as speeding and lack of negative safety signals) by decoupling behavior learning via next-token prediction from principle alignment via RL.

Insightful analysis of the failure mode of standard GRPO in multi-objective, safety-critical settings: group-wise variance normalization erases cross-group scale differences, suppressing optimization on rare catastrophic events. VD-GRPO is a well-reasoned and effective remedy.
The dual-model rollout mechanism provides an effective and stable way to simulate reactive multi-agent interactions during RL fine-tuning without destabilizing non-ego dynamics.

Strong empirical performance on the nuPlan closed-loop benchmark, showing substantial improvements especially in realistic reactive settings (R-CLS) over strong baselines like Diffusion Planner and PLUTO.
Thorough ablation studies and analysis covering the impact of RL fine-tuning, variance decoupling, world model choice, group size, reward components, and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty of VD-GRPO is somewhat incremental, as removing or modifying the per-group standard deviation normalization has been explored in prior LLM literature (e.g., Dr.GRPO), though the motivation and application to multi-objective safety planning are well justified.
Evaluation of reactive driving in nuPlan relies primarily on IDM for surrounding vehicles, which has known behavioral limitations compared to true interactive multi-agent dynamics.
Minor presentation issues, such as referencing Figure 4 instead of Table 4 in Section B when discussing group size ablations, and a few typographical errors (e.g., 'fine-tuninig' on page 14).

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: decoupling trajectory generation into a behavioral pre-training stage (capturing multi-agent priors from demonstrations) and a rule-based reinforcement learning fine-tuning stage effectively addresses the issues of demonstration suboptimality (e.g., speeding, low TTC) and the lack of negative safety-critical data in expert datasets.

Insightful analysis of GRPO failure modes in multi-objective planning: the authors pinpoint that standard per-group variance normalization in GRPO equalizes advantage magnitudes across groups, causing rare safety-critical failures (collisions) to be drowned out by frequent, low-variance comfort variations. The proposed Variance-Decoupled GRPO (VD-GRPO) is simple, well-justified, and directly addresses this scale-erasure problem.

Practical dual-model simulation architecture: using a frozen copy of the pre-trained multi-agent motion predictor as a reactive world model allows interaction-aware exploration during RL without suffering from the non-reactivity of ground-truth replay or destabilizing non-ego dynamics.

Strong empirical performance on nuPlan: Plan-R1 achieves competitive results in non-reactive settings and noticeable improvements over prior learning-based planners (e.g., PLUTO, Diffusion Planner) in the challenging reactive closed-loop benchmark (Test14-hard and Test14-random).

Thorough ablation studies: the paper provides comprehensive ablations covering the contribution of RL fine-tuning, the difference between standard GRPO and VD-GRPO, group size G, KL penalty β, reward scaling c, reactive world modeling vs. GT replay, and individual reward terms.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty in RL optimization: VD-GRPO primarily removes the group-wise standard deviation normalization and replaces it with a fixed scaling constant. This formulation is functionally equivalent to classical REINFORCE with a group-mean baseline (or leave-one-out baseline), and closely mirrors recent modifications such as Dr.GRPO. While the domain-specific justification (multi-objective safety vs. comfort variance) is sound, the algorithmic contribution itself is incremental.

Potential metric alignment / benchmark overfitting: the rule-based rewards in Equation (3) (collision avoidance, drivable area compliance, speed limit compliance, comfort thresholds, and progress) closely mirror the exact scoring criteria and heuristics of the nuPlan benchmark. Fine-tuning directly on the benchmark's scoring components makes it unclear whether the model has genuinely learned safe and generalized driving policies or is exploiting specific nuances of the nuPlan simulation rules.

Sim-to-real and compounding error concerns in the reactive world model: the frozen autoregressive agent model used as the simulation world model is relatively small (5M parameters) and trained via imitation. When the ego policy explores novel trajectories during RL, out-of-distribution queries may lead to compounding errors or unrealistic reactive behaviors from the surrounding agents, which is not quantitatively evaluated.

Credit assignment across sequence tokens: trajectory-level objectives (such as progress and speed limit compliance) are handled by uniformly broadcasting the scalar trajectory score across all constituent tokens. While empirically workable, this lacks temporal credit assignment and could introduce gradient misattribution across different phases of a maneuver.
